questions.question: What causes Leontes to turn against Hermione and Polixenes?

options.text: He interprets their friendly behavior as an affair.
He discovers they have stolen the royal treasury.
He learns that they have imprisoned Mamillius.
He receives proof that Camillo has crowned Polixenes.

questions.explanation: Seeing Hermione's warmth toward Polixenes, Leontes turns hospitality into grounds for jealousy.

evidence.exact:
LEONTES.
[Aside.] Too hot, too hot!
To mingle friendship far is mingling bloods.
I have tremor cordis on me. My heart dances,
But not for joy,—not joy. This entertainment
May a free face put on, derive a liberty
From heartiness, from bounty, fertile bosom,
And well become the agent: ’t may, I grant:
But to be paddling palms and pinching fingers,
As now they are, and making practis’d smiles
As in a looking-glass; and then to sigh, as ’twere
The mort o’ th’ deer. O, that is entertainment
My bosom likes not, nor my brows. Mamillius,
Art thou my boy?

questions.question: What does Camillo do when Leontes orders him to poison Polixenes?

options.text: He asks Antigonus to carry out the killing.
He warns Polixenes and helps him escape.
He poisons Hermione instead of Polixenes.
He hands Polixenes over to the Queen's guards.

questions.explanation: Camillo reveals the murder order to Polixenes rather than obey it, and leaves with him.

evidence.exact:
CAMILLO.
I am appointed him to murder you.

Apollo, pardon
My great profaneness ’gainst thine oracle!
I’ll reconcile me to Polixenes,
New woo my queen,	 recall the good Camillo,
Whom I proclaim a man of truth, of mercy;
For, being transported by my jealousies
To bloody thoughts and to revenge, I chose
Camillo for the minister to poison
My friend Polixenes: which had been done,
But that the good mind of Camillo tardied
My swift command, though I with death and with
Reward did threaten and encourage him,
Not doing it and being done. He, most humane
And fill’d with honour, to my kingly guest
Unclasp’d my practice, quit his fortunes here,
Which you knew great, and to the certain hazard
Of all incertainties himself commended,
No richer than his honour. How he glisters
Thorough my rust! And how his piety
Does my deeds make the blacker!

questions.question: What does Apollo's oracle declare about Hermione's case?

options.text: Camillo has secretly fathered the abandoned baby.
Leontes must choose a new wife before ruling again.
Hermione is innocent and Leontes is a jealous tyrant.
Hermione and Polixenes must both be condemned.

questions.explanation: The oracle vindicates Hermione, Polixenes, Camillo, and the baby while condemning Leontes's jealousy.

evidence.exact:
OFFICER.
[Reads.] “Hermione is chaste; Polixenes blameless; Camillo a true subject; Leontes a jealous tyrant; his innocent babe truly begotten; and the king shall live without an heir, if that which is lost be not found.”

questions.question: What news finally makes Leontes recognize his injustice during the trial?

options.text: Polixenes has returned with an invading army.
Antigonus has brought the baby back to court.
Florizel has renounced his claim to Bohemia.
Mamillius has died from distress over his mother.

questions.explanation: After rejecting the oracle, Leontes hears that his son is dead and admits that heaven strikes at his injustice.

evidence.exact:
SERVANT.
O sir, I shall be hated to report it.
The prince your son, with mere conceit and fear
Of the queen’s speed, is gone.

LEONTES.
Apollo’s angry, and the heavens themselves
Do strike at my injustice.

questions.question: What happens to Antigonus after he leaves the baby on the Bohemian coast?

options.text: A bear pursues and kills him.
The shepherd arrests him for stealing sheep.
Polixenes appoints him guardian of Florizel.
He sails back to Sicilia with Camillo.

questions.explanation: Antigonus exits pursued by a bear; the Clown later describes the animal eating him.

evidence.prefix:
the chase:
I am gone for ever.

evidence.exact:
CLOWN.
Go you the next way with your findings. I’ll go see if the bear be gone from the gentleman, and how much he hath eaten. They are never curst but when they are hungry: if there be any of him left, I’ll bury it.

questions.question: Who takes pity on the abandoned baby and brings her into a new household?

options.text: Autolycus, who returns her directly to Leontes.
An old shepherd who finds her near the shore.
Camillo, who carries her to Polixenes's court.
Polixenes, who recognizes her as a princess.

questions.explanation: The shepherd discovers the child and says he will take her up out of pity.

evidence.exact: Mercy on ’s, a bairn! A very pretty bairn! A boy or a child, I wonder? A pretty one; a very pretty one. Sure, some scape. Though I am not bookish, yet I can read waiting-gentlewoman in the scape. This has been some stair-work, some trunk-work, some behind-door-work. They were warmer that got this than the poor thing is here. I’ll take it up for pity: yet I’ll tarry till my son come; he halloed but even now. Whoa-ho-hoa!

questions.question: Why does Polixenes oppose Florizel's marriage to Perdita at the sheep-shearing feast?

options.text: He fears Perdita will inherit the throne of Sicilia.
He has promised Florizel to Paulina that morning.
He believes a shepherd's daughter is beneath the royal heir.
He knows Perdita has already married Camillo.

questions.explanation: Polixenes contrasts the heir's sceptre with a shepherd's staff and threatens to disinherit his son.

evidence.exact:
POLIXENES.
[Discovering himself.] Mark your divorce, young sir,
Whom son I dare not call; thou art too base
To be acknowledged: thou a sceptre’s heir,
That thus affects a sheep-hook! Thou, old traitor,
I am sorry that, by hanging thee, I can
But shorten thy life one week. And thou, fresh piece
Of excellent witchcraft, whom of force must know
The royal fool thou cop’st with,—
evidence.prefix:
e must not.
Mark our contract.

evidence.exact:
POLIXENES.
I’ll have thy beauty scratch’d with briers and made
More homely than thy state. For thee, fond boy,
If I may ever know thou dost but sigh
That thou no more shalt see this knack (as never
I mean thou shalt), we’ll bar thee from succession;
Not hold thee of our blood, no, not our kin,
Far than Deucalion off. Mark thou my words.
Follow us to the court. Thou churl, for this time,
Though full of our displeasure, yet we free thee
From the dead blow of it. And you, enchantment,
Worthy enough a herdsman; yea, him too
That makes himself, but for our honour therein,
Unworthy thee. If ever henceforth thou
These rural latches to his entrance open,
Or hoop his body more with thy embraces,
I will devise a death as cruel for thee
As thou art tender to ’t.

questions.question: Where does Camillo advise Florizel and Perdita to seek protection after the feast?

options.text: At the temple in Delphos as prisoners.
At Polixenes's court under their true names.
At Antigonus's house on the Bohemian shore.
At Leontes's court in Sicilia.

questions.explanation: Camillo directs their flight to Sicilia and expects Leontes to welcome them.

evidence.exact:
CAMILLO.
Then list to me:
This follows, if you will not change your purpose,
But undergo this flight, make for Sicilia,
And there present yourself and your fair princess,
For so, I see, she must be, ’fore Leontes:
She shall be habited as it becomes
The partner of your bed. Methinks I see
Leontes opening his free arms and weeping
His welcomes forth; asks thee, the son, forgiveness,
As ’twere i’ th’ father’s person; kisses the hands
Of your fresh princess; o’er and o’er divides him
’Twixt his unkindness and his kindness. Th’ one
He chides to hell, and bids the other grow
Faster than thought or time.

questions.question: What helps establish that Perdita is Leontes and Hermione's lost daughter?

options.text: The mantle, jewel, and Antigonus's letters found with her.
A marriage contract signed by Polixenes at the feast.
A confession that Autolycus raised her at the palace.
A message naming her in Florizel's military orders.

questions.explanation: The preserved objects and letters, together with her resemblance to Hermione, establish Perdita's identity.

evidence.exact:
THIRD GENTLEMAN.
Most true, if ever truth were pregnant by circumstance. That which you hear you’ll swear you see, there is such unity in the proofs. The mantle of Queen Hermione’s, her jewel about the neck of it, the letters of Antigonus found with it, which they know to be his character; the majesty of the creature in resemblance of the mother, the affection of nobleness which nature shows above her breeding, and many other evidences proclaim her with all certainty to be the king’s daughter. Did you see the meeting of the two kings?
evidence.prefix: . Has the king found his heir?

questions.question: What does Hermione reveal after the apparent statue comes to life?

options.text: She has never heard the oracle concerning the lost child.
She has preserved herself in hope of seeing her daughter again.
She has spent the years ruling Bohemia in disguise.
She has returned only to demand Florizel's punishment.

questions.explanation: Hermione says Paulina told her the oracle offered hope that Perdita lived, and she kept herself alive to see the outcome.

evidence.exact:
HERMIONE.
You gods, look down,
And from your sacred vials pour your graces
Upon my daughter’s head! Tell me, mine own,
Where hast thou been preserv’d? where liv’d? how found
Thy father’s court? for thou shalt hear that I,
Knowing by Paulina that the oracle
Gave hope thou wast in being, have preserv’d
Myself to see the issue.
